en: The Mirror of Cāṇakya’s Ethics, Chapter One:
Having bowed my head to Viṣṇu, the Lord and Sovereign of the three worlds;
I shall declare a compendium of the principles of statecraft, extracted from various treatises. (1)

Having studied this according to the scriptures, O best of beings, a man understands what is prescribed by dharma, as well as what should and should not be done, and what is auspicious and inauspicious. (2)
Therefore, out of a desire for the welfare of the world, I shall fully explain that by the mere knowledge of which one attains omniscience. (3)
Even a wise man comes to grief through instructing foolish disciples, supporting wicked women, and associating with those who are miserable. (4)
A wicked wife, a deceitful friend, a servant who speaks back, and living in a house with snakes—these are nothing but death; of this there is no doubt.
One should save wealth for times of distress; one should protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
and one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth. (6)
One should save wealth for times of misfortune; for how can calamities befall the prosperous?
Fortune is sometimes fickle, and even that which has been accumulated may perish. (7)
In that country where there is no respect, no livelihood, no kinsmen, and even no acquisition of knowledge, one should not make one's residence. (8)
A creditor, a learned priest, a king, a river, and a physician as the fifth—if these five are not found in a place, one should not dwell there for even a single day. ||9||
Where the five—worldly conduct, fear, shame, courtesy, and a disposition toward renunciation—are not found, one should not make one's dwelling there. 1.10
One should know servants by their obedience in being sent on errands, kinsmen by their presence at the onset of misfortune, a friend in times of calamity, and a wife when wealth has been exhausted.
He who stands by one when afflicted by illness, when calamity has arrived, during famine, in the perils of enemies, at the royal court, or in the cremation ground—he alone is a kinsman. (12)
He who abandons certainties and pursues uncertainties loses his certainties; for that which is uncertain is already lost. 13.
A wise man should marry a girl born of a noble family, even if she is ugly;
one should not marry a girl of beautiful form and good character from a low-born family, but rather from a family of equal status.
One should never place trust in rivers, those with weapons in hand, clawed creatures, horned animals, nor in women and royal households. (15)
Nectar should be taken even from poison; gold even from filth;
good conduct even from an enemy; and a well-spoken word even from a child. (16)
The food of women is said to be twofold, their modesty fourfold, their recklessness sixfold, and their passion eightfold. (17)
Thus ends the first chapter in the Cāṇakyanītidarpaṇa. ||1||
The Second Chapter. Untruthfulness, rashness, deceit, foolishness, excessive greed, impurity, and mercilessness are the innate defects of women. (1)
Delicious food, the power to enjoy it, beautiful women, the power for sexual pleasure, wealth, and the power to give charity—these are not the fruits of meager austerity. (2)
He whose son is self-controlled, whose wife follows his will,
and who is content with his wealth— his heaven is indeed right here on earth.
They are sons who are devoted to their father; he is a father who provides nourishment.
He is a friend in whom there is trust; she is a wife in whom there is peace.
One should avoid such a friend who destroys one's interests in one's absence but speaks kindly in one's presence; he is like a jar of poison with milk on its surface.
One should not trust a bad friend, nor should one trust even a good friend;
for a friend, when provoked to anger, might reveal all one's secrets. (6)
One should not reveal with speech an action contemplated in the mind;
one should protect it secretly through counsel and then employ it in action.
Folly is indeed a misery, and youth is indeed a misery;
but living in another's house is a misery even more miserable than misery. (8)
There is not a maṇikya on every mountain, nor a pearl in every elephant; indeed, there are no holy men everywhere, nor sandalwood in every forest. (9)
Sons should always be directed toward various virtues by the wise;
those who are knowledgeable in ethics and endowed with good character become honored by their family. 2.10

A mother who does not teach her children is an enemy, and a father who does not teach them is a foe; those who are uneducated do not shine in the midst of an assembly, just as a crane does not shine among swans. 11.
There are many faults in pampering and many virtues in striking;
therefore, one should strike both the student and the son, but not pamper them.
One should make each day fruitful through acts of giving, study, and ritual practice— whether by means of a verse, half a verse, or even half of a half-verse.
Separation from a beloved, humiliation by one's own kin, a remaining debt, service to a wicked king, and a friend who turns away due to poverty—these five burn the body even without fire. (14)
Trees on the riverbank, women in the houses of others, and kings devoid of ministers—these undoubtedly perish quickly. 15.
The strength of Brahmins is knowledge, the strength of kings is their army, the strength of Vaiśyas is wealth, and the strength of Śūdras is service. (16)
A courtesan abandons a man who has no wealth, subjects abandon a king who has been defeated,
birds abandon a tree that is devoid of fruit, and a guest abandons a house after having eaten.
Having received their sacrificial fee, the Brahmins abandon the patron;
likewise, students who have acquired knowledge leave their teacher, and deer desert a forest that has been scorched. (18)
A man who forms friendship with one who is ill-behaved, of evil vision, difficult to dwell with, and wicked, perishes quickly. (19)
Affection shines in a person of equal status; service shines in a king;
trade shines in business dealings; and a divine woman shines in the home. (2.20)
Thus ends the second chapter in the Cāṇakyanītidarpaṇa. ||2||
The Third Chapter:
In whose family is there no fault? Who has not been afflicted by disease?
By whom has misfortune not been encountered? And for whom is there constant happiness? (1)
Conduct reveals one's lineage; speech reveals one's country;
agitation reveals affection; and the body reveals one's diet. (2)
One should marry one's daughter into a noble family and establish one's son in the sciences; one should involve an enemy in vice and engage a friend in dharma. (3)
Between a wicked person and a serpent, the serpent is better than the wicked person;
for the serpent bites only at the proper time, whereas the wicked person strikes at every step. (4)
For this purpose, kings gather together those of noble birth;
they do not undergo any change of character in the beginning, middle, or end. (5)
It is said that at the time of universal dissolution, the oceans indeed break their bounds; yet the virtuous do not seek to transgress their limits even in the dissolution.
A fool, however, should be struck; he is a two-legged beast manifest before one's eyes.
He is pierced by the arrow of words, like an invisible thorn.
Those endowed with beauty and youth, born of noble lineage, do not shine if devoid of learning, just like *kiṃśuka* flowers without fragrance. (8)
The beauty of cuckoos is their song; the beauty of women is their devotion to their husbands; the beauty of the ugly is learning; and the beauty of ascetics is forbearance. (9)
One should abandon an individual for the sake of a family; one should abandon a family for the sake of a village;
one should abandon a village for the sake of a country; and one should abandon the whole earth for the sake of the self. (3.10)
In exertion there is no poverty; for one who recites prayers, there is no sin;
through silence, there is no quarrel; and for one who remains awake, there is no fear. (11)
Sītā was ruined by excessive beauty, Rāvaṇa by excessive pride, and Bali was bound because of excessive generosity; therefore, one should avoid extremes in all things.
What indeed is too heavy for the capable? What is too far for the industrious? What is a foreign land for those with true knowledge? Who is a stranger to those who speak kindly? (13)
Even by a single well-grown tree, flowering and fragrant, that entire forest is perfumed, just as a family is by a good son. (14)
Just as an entire forest is consumed by fire ignited from a single dry tree, so too is an entire family destroyed by a wicked son. 15.
By even a single good son who is virtuous and endowed with learning, the entire family is gladdened, just as the night is by the moon. (16)
What is the use of many sons born who only cause grief and torment? Better is one son who supports the lineage, upon whom the family finds its rest.
One should fondle [the son] for five years, and for ten years one should discipline him;
but when the sixteenth year has arrived, one should behave toward the son as toward a friend. 18.
In times of calamity, during the onset of another's power, in a famine, in the face of terrifying danger, and in the company of wicked people—he who flees survives. (19)
For him in whom not even one among dharma, artha, kāma, or mokṣa is found, there is nothing but death throughout birth after birth among mortals. (3.20)
Where fools are not honored, where grain is well-stored, and where there is no quarreling between husband and wife—there Fortune has come of her own accord. (21)
Thus ends the third chapter in the Cāṇakyanītidarpaṇa. ||3||
The Fourth Chapter:
Lifespan, action, wealth, knowledge, and even death—these five are indeed created for the embodied being while still dwelling in the womb. (1)
Sons, friends, and kinsmen turn away from you when you are virtuous;
yet those who would go with you [to the next world] are the family’s merits resulting from that dharma.
Just as the fish, the tortoise, and the bird protect their young constantly through sight, meditation, and touch, so too does association with the virtuous. ||3||
As long as this body remains healthy and death is still far off, one should perform what is beneficial for the self; for what will one do when the end of life has come? (4)
Knowledge indeed possesses the qualities of the wish-fulfilling cow, for it yields fruit even out of season;
like a mother during travel, knowledge is remembered as hidden wealth. (5)
Even a single son who possesses virtue is better than a hundred who lack it;
a single moon dispels the darkness, whereas thousands of stars cannot.
A fool, though born, lives long; therefore, it is better that he dies at birth.
He who dies suffers but little pain, whereas the dull-witted man burns with misery for as long as he lives. (7)
Dwelling in a wretched village, serving a family of low birth, poor food, a wife with a wrathful face,
a foolish son, and a widowed daughter.
Without fire, these six burn the body. ||8||
What is the use of that cow which neither gives milk nor bears calves?
What is the purpose of a son who is born but is neither learned nor devoted? (9)
For those scorched by the miseries of saṃsāra, there are three causes of rest:
offspring, a wife, and association with the virtuous. (4.10)
Kings speak but once; the wise speak but once;
daughters are given away but once—these three things happen only once. (11)
Austerity is for one alone; study is for two; singing is for three;
traveling is for four; a field is for five; and battle is for many. 12.
She is a wife who is pure and skillful; she is a wife who is devoted to her husband;
she is a wife who is dear to her husband; she is a wife who speaks the truth. (13)
The home of one without a son is empty; the quarters are empty for one without kinsmen;
the heart of a fool is empty; but poverty is the emptiness of all things. (14)
Scripture is poison without practice; food is poison when undigested;
social gathering is poison for the poor; and a young woman is poison for the old. (15)
One should abandon dharma devoid of compassion; one should abandon a teacher devoid of knowledge;
one should abandon a wife whose face is set in anger; and one should abandon kinsmen who lack affection. (16)
For embodied beings, old age is the passage of time; for mountains, water is their decay.
For women, lack of sexual union is old age; for the mind, the arrow of harsh words is its decay. 17.
"What is the time? Who are my friends? What is the place? What are my expenditures and income? And who am I, and what is my power?"—this should be reflected upon again and again. (18)
Agni is the deity of the twice-born; for sages, he is the divinity within the heart;
for those of small intellect, he resides in images; but for those who see with equanimity, he is everywhere. 19.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Cāṇakyanītidarpaṇa. ||4||
The Fifth Chapter:
Fire is the preceptor of the twice-born; among the social orders, the Brāhmaṇa is the preceptor;
the husband alone is the preceptor of women; and the guest is the preceptor of all. (1)
Just as gold is tested by four means— rubbing, cutting, heating, and striking—
so too is a person tested by four means.
By renunciation, by moral conduct, by virtue, and by action. ||2||
One should fear as long as danger has not yet arrived;
but having seen that danger has arrived, one should strike back without hesitation.
Those born from the same womb and born under the same constellation do not become equal in their conduct, just like the jujube fruit and its thorns.
One who is free from desire shall not be an official; one who lacks longing shall not be fond of ornaments;
one who is unrefined shall not speak kindly; and one who speaks clearly shall not be a deceiver.
The learned are hated by fools; the very wealthy are hated by the poor; women of noble family are hated by those who covet others' wives; and the unfortunate are hated by the fortunate. (6)
Knowledge that has fallen into indolence, wealth that has passed into the hands of others, a field sown with few seeds, and an army without a leader—all these are lost. (7)
Knowledge is maintained through practice; a family is maintained by character;
a noble person is known by their virtues; and anger is perceived by the eyes. (8)
Dharma is protected by wealth; knowledge is protected by practice;
a king is protected by mildness; and a household is protected by a virtuous wife. (9)
The Vedic scriptures are one way, and the scholarly wisdom derived from them is another;
that state of peace is yet another, while people suffer in still another way. (5.10)
Generosity destroys poverty; ethical discipline destroys the miserable states of existence;
wisdom destroys ignorance; and meditative cultivation destroys fear. //11//
There is no disease equal to desire; there is no enemy equal to delusion;
there is no fire equal to anger; and there is no happiness higher than knowledge. 12.
For one alone undergoes birth and death; one alone experiences the auspicious and the inauspicious;
one alone falls into the hells, and one alone attains the supreme goal. (13)
To the knower of Brahman, heaven is as a blade of grass; to the hero, life is as a blade of grass;
to one who has conquered his desires, a woman is as a blade of grass; and to the dispassionate man, the entire world is as a blade of grass. 14.
Knowledge is a friend during travels, and a wife is a friend in the home;
medicine is a friend for the sick, and dharma is a friend to the deceased. 15.
Rain upon the oceans is in vain; food for one who is already satiated is in vain;
a gift given by one who is capable [of providing more] is in vain; and a lamp during the day is also in vain. (16)
There is no water equal to the cloud; there is no strength equal to one's own self;
there is no brilliance equal to the eye; there is no object as dear as grain. 17.
The destitute desire wealth, and four-footed creatures desire speech;
human beings desire heaven, and the gods desire liberation.
By truth the earth is sustained; by truth the sun gives heat;
by truth the wind blows; everything is established in truth. ||19||
Fortune is fickle, the vital breaths are fickle, and life in this body is fickle;
in this ever-shifting cycle of existence, dharma alone is indeed immovable.
Among men, the barber is the rogue; among birds, it is the crow;
among quadrupeds, it is the jackal; and among women, the rogue is Mālinī.
The progenitor, the one who performs the initiation, the one who imparts knowledge, the giver of food, and the protector from fear—these five are remembered as fathers. ||22||
The wife of a king, the wife of a preceptor, the wife of a friend, as well as the mother of one's wife, and one's own mother—these five are remembered as mothers. (23)
Fifth Chapter;
Sixth Chapter:
Having heard the Dharma, one understands it; having heard it, one abandons evil-mindedness.
By hearing it one attains knowledge; by hearing it one may attain liberation. ||1||
Among birds, the crow is the outcaste; among animals, the dog is the outcaste;
among sages, the sinful man is the outcaste; and one who reviles all outcastes is the ultimate outcaste. ||2||
Bell-metal is purified by ash; copper is purified by acid;
a woman is purified by her menses; and a river is purified by its current. (3)
A king is honored while wandering; a twice-born man is honored while wandering;
a yogi is honored while wandering; but a woman perishes by wandering. ||4||
He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen.
He who has wealth is a man in this world; he who has wealth is a wise man.
The intellect arises as such, the resolve is likewise such, and the companions are exactly such as the destiny itself may be. (6)
Time ripens all beings; Time destroys all creatures.
Time remains awake while others sleep; indeed, Time is difficult to overcome. (7)
One born blind does not see; one blinded by desire does not see at all;
those intoxicated by pride do not see; and one who is greedy does not see a fault. (8)
The self performs the action itself; the self experiences its fruit itself;
the self wanders in saṃsāra itself; and the self is liberated from it itself. (9)
The king bears the sin committed by the kingdom; the domestic priest bears the sin of the king;
the husband bears the sin committed by the wife; and likewise, the teacher bears the sin of the disciple. (6.10)
A father who incurs debt is an enemy; a mother who is unfaithful is an enemy;
a beautiful wife is an enemy; and an unlearned son is an enemy. (11)
One should win over the greedy with wealth, the stubborn with a gesture of salutation (añjali),
the fool by following his whims, and the wise man by speaking the truth.
Better is no kingdom than the kingdom of a bad king; better is no friend than the friendship of a bad friend;
better is no disciple than the discipleship of a bad disciple.
Better is no wife at all than a wife who is a bad wife. ||13||
How can there be happiness for the subjects under the rule of a bad king?
How can there be fulfillment with a bad friend as a friend? And how can there be delight in the home with bad wives?
For one who teaches a bad student to another bad student, whence can there be fame? ||14||
One should learn one quality from the lion, one from the crane, four from the cock, five from the crow, six from the dog, and three from the donkey. (15)
Whatever task a man desires to perform, whether it be great or small, he should accomplish that undertaking with total exertion; this alone is declared to be the way of the lion. (16)
Having restrained the senses and being free from attachment and aversion, equanimous in pain and pleasure, and tranquil—the knower of reality is called a virtuous person. (17)
One should learn four things from a cock: rising up at the proper time, fighting, sharing with kinsmen, and eating only after having seized [the prey] oneself. //18//
One should learn five things from a crow: the practice of secret mating, gathering at the proper times, vigilance, and mistrust. (19)
Eating much, being easily satisfied, sleeping soundly, having a quick wit, devotion to one's master, and bravery—these six qualities of a dog are [lacking] in him. (6.20)
Though exhausted, he carries his burden; he notices neither cold nor heat;
he always moves about contented—one should learn these three things from the donkey. (21)
The man who practices these twenty qualities in all circumstances of action shall become invincible.
Chapter Seven: A wise person should not disclose the loss of wealth, mental anguish, domestic misconduct, deception, or humiliation. (1)
In the employment of wealth and grain, in the acquisition of knowledge,
in eating, and in worldly dealings, one who has cast off shame shall be happy.
The happiness and peace that belong to those satisfied by the nectar of contentment do not belong to those greedy for wealth, who run hither and thither.
One should practice contentment in three things: one's own wife, food, and wealth; and one should certainly not practice contentment in three others: study, recitation of mantras, and giving.
One should not pass between two Brahmins, nor between a Brahmin and fire, nor between a husband and wife, nor between a master and a servant, nor between a plow and its oxen.
One should not touch with one's feet fire, a teacher, or a Brāhmaṇa;
nor indeed a cow, a young girl, an elder, or likewise a child.
One should abandon a cart with five cubits, a horse with ten cubits, an elephant with a thousand cubits, and a wicked person by abandoning the entire country. (7)
An elephant is controlled by a mere goad, a horse is struck with the hand, a horned beast with a staff in hand, and a wicked person with a sword in hand. (8)
Brahmins find satisfaction in food, peacocks in the thundering of clouds; the virtuous rejoice in the prosperity of others, while the wicked rejoice in the misfortunes of others.
One should subdue a powerful person by conciliation, a wicked person by opposition,
and an enemy of equal strength either through diplomacy or by force.
The strength of kings is the power of their arms; the strength of a Brahmin is the power of his knowledge of Brahman; and for women, beauty, youth, and sweetness are the unsurpassed strength. (11)
One should not be excessively upright; go and look at the forest region!
There the straight trees are cut down, while the crooked trees remain standing. (12)
Where there is water, there the swans dwell;
likewise, they avoid what is dry.
A man should not be like a swan.
Again they abandon [them], and again they take recourse [to them]. ||13||
Indeed, the relinquishing of accumulated wealth is its true preservation, just as an overflow channel is for the waters contained within a reservoir. (14)
He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen. He who has wealth is a man in this world; he who has wealth truly lives. (15)
Four signs of those who dwell in heaven reside here in the body within this world of living beings:
a devotion to giving and sweet speech.
Worship of the gods and the gratification of Brahmins. ||16||
Excessive anger, harsh speech, poverty, enmity toward one's own kin,
association with the base, and service to those of low birth.
These are the marks on the bodies of those residing in hell. ||17||
If one goes to the lion’s palace,
one obtains the pearls from the frontal globes of elephants; but when one has gone to the den of jackals, what can be obtained?
The tearing of a calf's tail and a donkey's hide. ||18||
Life without knowledge is as useless as a dog's tail;
it is incapable of guarding secrets, nor is it able to ward off stings. (19)
Purity of speech, purity of mind, restraint of the senses, and the purity of compassion toward all beings—this is the purity for those who seek the highest goal. 7.20.
As one perceives fragrance in a flower, oil in sesame, fire in wood, clarified butter in milk, and molasses in sugarcane, so should one perceive the Self within the body through discernment. 21.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Cāṇakyanītidarpaṇa. ||7||
The Eighth Chapter:
The base desire wealth; the mediocre desire both wealth and honor;
the superior desire honor alone, for honor is indeed the wealth of the great. (1)
Even after consuming sugarcane, water, milk, roots, betel, fruit, or medicine, one must still perform such rites as bathing and giving gifts. (2)
A lamp consumes darkness and produces soot;
whatever food one constantly eats, such is the offspring that is born.
O wise one, bestow wealth upon those endowed with virtue, and never give it elsewhere; for the water obtained from the ocean at the mouth of a cloud is always possessed of sweetness,
having sustained all living beings, both stationary and moving, across the entire circle of the earth.
Behold again that very same ocean as it approaches, multiplied ten millionfold.
Even by thousands of Cāṇḍālas and by wise seers who perceive the truth, a single Yavana is declared to be low-born; indeed, there is no one more base than a Yavana.
After anointing with oil, exposure to the smoke of a funeral pyre, sexual intercourse, or the act of shaving,
one remains an outcaste (caṇḍāla) until one performs a ritual bath.
Water is medicine when food is undigested; water bestows strength when food is digested.
Water is nectar during a meal, and it removes poison at the end of a meal.
Knowledge devoid of action is lost, and a man is lost through ignorance;
an army without a leader is lost, for women are indeed lost when they are without a husband. (8)
A wife who dies in old age, wealth that has fallen into the hands of kinsmen, and food dependent on others—these three are the humiliations of men. (9)
Without the Agnihotra there are no Vedas, nor is there action without giving; there is no accomplishment without devotion; therefore, devotion is indeed the cause. ||8.10||
The deity is not found in wood, nor in stone, nor in clay;
for the deity is found in devotion, therefore devotion is indeed the cause.
By performing service with devotion toward images made of wood, stone, or metal,
and likewise with faith, one attains success through the grace of Viṣṇu.
By performing service with devotion using materials such as wood, stone, or metal, and likewise with faith, one attains success through the grace of Viṣṇu. ||13||
There is no austerity equal to tranquility; there is no happiness higher than contentment; there is no disease greater than craving; and there is no dharma superior to compassion. (14)
Virtue adorns physical beauty; character adorns one's lineage;
mastery adorns knowledge; and enjoyment adorns wealth. ||15||
The form of one devoid of virtue is ruined; the family of one of ill-conduct is ruined; the learning of one who has not achieved mastery is ruined; and wealth is ruined by lack of enjoyment. 16.
Pure is the water found on the ground; pure is the woman devoted to her husband;
pure is the king who ensures security; and pure is the Brahmin who is contented. (17)
The twice-born have perished through lack of contentment, and kings through excessive contentment;
the courtesan has perished through modesty, and the noble wife through shamelessness. (18)
Of what use is a vast lineage if it is devoid of learning for embodied beings?
Even one of low birth who is wise is honored even by the gods. (19)
The learned man is praised in the world; the learned man is honored everywhere. Through knowledge one obtains everything; knowledge is honored everywhere. 8.20
Those endowed with beauty and youth, born of a noble lineage, do not shine if they are devoid of learning, just like *kiṃśuka* flowers without fragrance. (21)
Indeed, the earth is burdened by those who eat meat, drink liquor, and speak words devoid of refinement— beasts in human form.
A sacrifice lacking food burns the kingdom; one lacking mantras burns the officiating priests;
and one lacking gifts burns the patron. There is no enemy equal to a sacrifice [performed] thus.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Cāṇakyanītidarpaṇa*. ||8||
The Ninth Chapter:
O dear one, if you desire liberation, abandon sense-objects like poison;
drink in forgiveness, uprightness, compassion, purity, and truth as if they were nectar. (1)
Those lowest of men who speak of each other's vital secrets meet their own destruction, like snakes in the belly of an anthill.
Fragrance was placed in gold, fruit in the sugarcane stalk, and indeed no flower in sandalwood; likewise, the wise man, the wealthy man, and the king are long-lived.
In former times, no one among the elements was a bestower of enlightenment. ||3||
Among all medicinal herbs, the amṛtā is preeminent; among all forms of happiness, food is preeminent;
among all the sense faculties, the eye is preeminent.
Among all the limbs, the head is the most important. ||4||
A messenger does not travel through the sky, nor can news move there; this was never spoken before, nor is there any meeting [there].
Yet, the eclipses of the sun and moon situated in the firmament are auspicious.
How can that best of the twice-born who knows this not be a wise man? ||5||
A student, a servant, a traveler, one afflicted by hunger, one terrified by fear, a storekeeper, and a doorkeeper—these seven should be awakened from sleep. (6)
One should not awaken seven who are sleeping: a snake, a king, a tiger, an elderly person, a child, another's dog, and a fool.
And those twice-born ones by whom the Vedas have been only half-studied, as well as those who eat the food of Śūdras—what will they accomplish? They are like serpents deprived of their venom. (8)
When he is angry there is no fear, and when he is pleased there is no acquisition of wealth;
since there is neither punishment nor favor, what will he do when he is enraged? (9)
Even a snake that is without venom must spread its great hood;
whether it possesses poison or not, it must display a terrifying display of its hoods.
The time of the wise passes away through devotion to Vedic study in the morning, through devotion to women at midday, and through devotion to charity at night. (11)
A garland strung by one’s own hand, sandalwood rubbed by one’s own hand, and a hymn written by one’s own hand—these would take away even the splendor of Śakra himself. (12)
Sugarcane stalks, sesame seeds, Shudras, a beloved woman, gold, and land; sandalwood, curd, betel leaf, and massage increase one's virtues. (13)
Poverty shines through fortitude;
the wearing of coarse garments shines through purity;
and the eating of poor food shines through its warmth.
Ugliness shines forth through the possession of virtuous conduct. ||14||
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Cāṇakyanītidarpaṇa. ||9||
The tenth chapter:
One who is destitute of wealth is not truly destitute, whereas one who possesses wealth is so only by certainty; however, he who is bereft of the jewel of knowledge is destitute of all things. (1)
One should place one's foot down purified by sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by scripture; and one should act with a mind that is purified. ||2||
If one seeks happiness, one should abandon knowledge; if one seeks knowledge, one should abandon happiness.
For one who seeks happiness, whence comes knowledge? For one who seeks knowledge, whence comes happiness? (3)
What do poets not see? What do crows not eat? What do drunkards not prattle? What do women not do? (4)
Fate makes a beggar a king and a king a mere beggar;
it makes a wealthy man penniless and a penniless man wealthy. (5)
To the greedy, a beggar is an enemy; to the foolish, an enlightener is a foe;
to women with paramours, a husband is an enemy; and to thieves, the moon is an adversary.
Those who possess neither learning nor austerity, neither generosity nor wisdom, neither virtuous conduct nor excellence, nor righteousness—
they are a mere burden upon the earth in the world of mortals.
Deer roam about in human form. ||7||
Instruction does not arise for those who lack inner substance;
by contact with the Malaya mountain, a bamboo stalk does not become sandalwood.
What can a treatise do for one who lacks wisdom within themselves?
What will a mirror avail a man who is deprived of his eyes? (9)
There is no means on this earth to turn a wicked person into a virtuous one;
even if the anus were washed a hundred times, it would not become a superior organ. || 10.10 ||
From hatred toward one's preceptor comes death; from hatred toward others, the loss of wealth;
from hatred toward the king, ruin; and from hatred toward a Brahmin, the destruction of the lineage. ||11||
Better is the forest inhabited by tigers and lordly elephants, where one dwells among trees, subsisting on leaves, fruits, and water,
sleeping upon grass, and wearing a hundred worn-out bark garments.
One does not lead a life destitute of wealth in the midst of kinsmen. ||12||
The Brahmin is a tree; its root is the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), its branches are the Vedas, and its leaves are the ritual acts of dharma.
Therefore, the root must be protected with great effort.
When the root is severed, there are neither branches nor leaves. ||13||
My mother is the goddess Kamalā, my father is Lord Janārdana, my kinsmen are the devotees of Viṣṇu, and my own country is the three worlds. (14)
Birds of various colors perched upon a single tree depart toward the ten directions at dawn; what cause for lamentation is there in that? (15)
He whose intellect is his strength—how can there be strength for one devoid of intellect?
For even a mad lion in the forest was brought down by a hare. (16)
"What concern is there for my life, if Hari is sung of as the sustainer of the universe?
Otherwise, how could he have created his mother’s breast-milk for the sake of the life of a mere infant?
Having reflected thus again and again, O Lord of the Yadus, O Lord of Lakṣmī, [I take refuge] in You alone.
I spend my time constantly in the service of your lotus feet. ||17||
Although my intellect is distinguished regarding the language of the gods (Sanskrit), I am nevertheless eager for other languages;
just as [there is a desire for] nectar among the immortals even when it exists.
There is a longing for the nectar of the lips of the women of heaven. ||18||
Flour is ten times more [efficacious] than grain; milk is ten times more than flour;
meat is eight times more than milk; and ghee is ten times more than meat. ||19||
Through grief diseases increase; through milk the body grows;
through ghee virility increases; from meat flesh increases. (10.20)
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Cāṇakyanītidarpaṇa. ||10||
Chapter Eleven:
Generosity, pleasant speech, fortitude, and discernment of what is appropriate—these four innate qualities are not acquired through practice. (1)
Having abandoned one's own faction, one should resort to the faction of others;
one perishes by oneself, just as a king does through unrighteousness.
The elephant has a massive body, yet it is subject to the goad; is the goad merely as large as the elephant?
When a lamp is ignited, darkness perishes; is the darkness merely as large as the lamp? Even when struck by a thunderbolt, mountains fall; are the mountains merely as large as the thunderbolt?
He whose splendor shines forth is powerful; what proof is there for [the existence of] gross things? ||3||
In the Kali age, Hari abandons the earth for ten thousand years;
half of that time [is spent by] the waters of the Ganges, and half of that by the village deities.
For one attached to the home there is no knowledge; for a meat-eater there is no compassion;
for one greedy for wealth there is no truth; and for one devoted to women there is no purity. (5)
A wicked person does not attain the state of a virtuous one,
even when instructed in many ways;
it is like a tree watered at its roots with milk and ghee.
A neem tree does not attain sweetness. ||6||
A wicked person whose impurity is internal is not purified even by hundreds of ritual baths at sacred fords,
just as a vessel that has held liquor is not cleansed even when it is burnt.
He who does not know the excellence of another's qualities always reviles him; there is nothing surprising in this,
just as a forest huntress reviles the pearls obtained from the frontal globes of an elephant.
Having abandoned the pearl, he wears the guñjā berry.
But those who always eat in silence for a full year are honored in the heavenly world for thousands of millions of yugas.
One who seeks knowledge should indeed avoid these eight: lust, anger, greed, delicacy of taste, vanity, curiosity, excessive sleep, and excessive indulgence. 11.10.
One who subsists on uncultivated roots and fruits, always delights in dwelling in the forest, and performs the *śrāddha* ceremony day after day— that one is called a brahmin sage (*ṛṣi*).
Content with eating only once a day, always devoted to the six duties,
and approaching his wife only during her season— that Brahmin is called a *dvija*.
He who is devoted to worldly occupations, who protects cattle, and who engages in the work of trade and agriculture—that brahmin is indeed called a vaiśya. (13)
A Brahmin who sells lac and other oils, indigo, saffron, honey, clarified butter, liquor, or meat is called a Śūdra. (14)
A Brahmin who thwarts the affairs of others, who is hypocritical, who pursues his own self-interest, who is deceitful, hateful, soft-spoken yet cruel, is called a "cat. (15)
That brahmin who, without any hesitation, destroys step-wells, wells, tanks, groves, and temples of the gods, is called a barbarian (mleccha). 16.

One who misappropriates the property of the gods or the property of the guru, who violates the wives of others, and who behaves with hostility toward all living beings—such a Brahmin is called a Cāṇḍāla. (17)
Wealth acquired through righteous deeds should be given away as food and charity; indeed, those who hoard it do not possess true prosperity.
Even today, the fame of Śrī Karṇa and Vikramāditya, the lord of power, endures, while our own long-accumulated wealth—devoid of the enjoyment of giving honey-like gifts—has long since perished.
Alas, flies are biting his own pair of feet, [which are as cool] as Nirvana! ||18||
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Cāṇakyanītidarpaṇa. ||11||
The twelfth chapter:
A joyful home, wise sons, a beloved wife who speaks sweetly,
wealth that fulfills one's desires, delight in one's own wife, and servants devoted to one's commands.
Hospitality, the daily worship of Śiva, sweet food and drink at home, and constant attendance upon the company of the virtuous—blessed indeed is the householder's stage of life! ||1||
O King, even a small gift that one endowed with compassion offers with faith to distressed Brahmins attains infinite and boundless merit.
That which is given [in such a manner] will not be obtained from the twice-born.
Courtesy toward one's own kin, compassion for strangers, constant guile toward the wicked, affection for the virtuous, pride before the base, and straightforwardness toward the learned;
valor toward enemies, forbearance toward elders, and craftiness toward women— [such is the conduct of the wise].
Thus, the stability of the world rests solely upon those men who are skilled in the arts. ||3||
My two hands are devoid of giving; my ears are enemies of sacred learning; my eyes are bereft of beholding the virtuous; my feet have never traveled to holy places;
my belly is filled with wealth acquired through injustice; and my head is held high with pride.
"O jackal, release it! Release it at once! This wretched and contemptible body! ||4||
Those men who possess no devotion for the lotus feet of the illustrious son of Yaśodā; whose sense of taste is not enamored with the narration of the virtues of the beloved of the cowherd girls;
and whose ears have no respect for the charmingly sweet stories of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s divine play—[for them, all is in vain].
"Fie on them! Fie on them! Fie on them!"—thus the mṛdaṅga drum, situated upon the platform for chanting, proclaims constantly. ||5||
When there is no leaf at all on the *karīra* tree, is it the fault of spring?
If even the owl does not see during the day, is it the fault of the sun? When rain does not fall into the mouth of the *cātaka* bird, is it the fault of the cloud?
Who is capable of erasing that which was previously inscribed on the forehead by destiny? ||6||
Indeed, through association with the virtuous, the wicked become good; but through association with the wicked, the virtuous do not become wicked.
Only clay can take on the fragrance born of flowers.
For flowers do not retain the fragrance of the soil. ||7||
Beholding the virtuous is meritorious, for the virtuous are themselves sacred pilgrimage sites;
a pilgrimage site bears fruit in time, but the company of the virtuous yields fruit immediately. (8)
O Brahmins, tell me: who is great in this city? A grove of palmyra trees.
Who is a donor? A washerman, for he gives back one's garment at night after having taken it in the morning. Who is skillful? Everyone is skillful at seizing the wealth and wives of others.
Why do you live, O friend? I live by the logic of the worm in poison. ||9||
They were not muddy with the water used for washing the feet of Brahmins,
nor resounded with the chanting of the Vedas and Shastras,
and they were devoid of the utterances of "Svaha" and "Svadha."
Those houses are equal to cremation grounds.
Truth is my mother, knowledge my father, righteousness my brother, compassion my friend, peace my wife, and forgiveness my son; these six are my kinsmen. (11)
Bodies are impermanent and worldly prosperity is never eternal;
death is always present—therefore, one must practice the accumulation of Dharma. 12.
Brahmins rejoice in invitations; cows rejoice in fresh grass;
a wife rejoices in her husband’s prosperity; and I rejoice in the feet of Kṛṣṇa. 13.
He who looks upon the wives of others as his own mother, upon the wealth of others as a clod of earth, and upon all beings as himself—he is a wise man. 14.
Devotion to the Dharma, sweetness of speech, enthusiasm for giving, sincerity toward friends, humility toward the guru, profound depth of heart,
purity in conduct, delight in virtue, and discernment regarding the scriptures.
O Rāghava, beauty resides in form and devotion resides in Śiva; yet, O Lord, it is in you that both truly exist. 15.
The wish-fulfilling tree has become mere wood; Mount Sumeru, the immovable, is but a stone; the wish-granting gem is a common rock;
the sun has lost its fierce rays; the moon is waning; the ocean is indeed salty;
Kāma is bodiless; Bali, the son of Diti, is a prisoner; and Nandin, who moves at will, is now a beast.
O Lord of the Raghus, I do not compare you to these; to whom could an analogy for you be given? (16)
Knowledge is a friend while traveling abroad, and a wife is a friend within the home;
medicine is a friend to the sick, and dharma is a friend to the deceased. (17)
One should learn discipline from princes, eloquent speech from the wise, falsehood from gamblers, and deceit from women. (18)
A man who spends without regard for his income, who is helpless, fond of quarreling, and afflicted in all his undertakings, perishes quickly. (19)
A wise person should not think of food; indeed, he should think only of the Dharma.
For food is born together with the birth of human beings.
In the investment of wealth and grain, in the acquisition of knowledge, as well as in eating and worldly dealings, one who has cast aside shame shall be happy. ||21||
A jar is gradually filled by the falling of drops of water;
that is the cause of all branches of knowledge, as well as of righteousness and wealth. (22)
Even in the decline of age, a wicked person remains indeed wicked; even when fully ripened, the *indravāruṇa* gourd does not attain sweetness.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Cāṇakyanītidarpaṇa*. 12.
Chapter Thirteen:
A man should live even for a single moment by means of pure action; he should not live even for an eon with a miserable life that opposes the interests of both worlds.
Grief for what has passed should not be made, nor should one worry about the future;
the wise conduct themselves according to the present time. ||2||
For gods, virtuous men, and fathers are pleased by one's inherent nature;
kinsmen by bathing and drinking; and the wise by the gift of speech. (3)
Oh, how wonderful are the deeds of the great-souled!
They regard prosperity as a mere blade of grass, yet they bow under its weight.
For whom there is affection, for him there is fear; affection is a vessel of suffering.
Sufferings have their root in affection; having abandoned them, one may dwell in happiness. (5)
The one who provides for the future and the one with presence of mind—these two prosper in happiness, while the fatalist perishes. (6)
The one who provides for the future and the one with presence of mind—these two prosper happily, while the fatalist perishes. (7)

When the queen is righteous, the subjects are most righteous; when she is sinful, they are sinful; when she is neutral, they are neutral. The subjects follow the king; as is the king, so are the subjects. (8)
I consider an embodied being devoid of dharma to be dead while living;
one who is endowed with dharma, though dead, is a long-lived person—of this there is no doubt.
For one in whom not even a single one of dharma, artha, kāma, or mokṣa is found, his birth is as useless as the fleshy protuberance on the neck of a goat. 13.10
Being scorched by the extremely intense fire of another's glory, the base, being unable to reach that same state, engage in slander. (11)
Attachment to sense objects leads to bondage; the mind free from sense objects leads to liberation.
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings. 12.
When identification with the body has dissolved through knowledge into the Supreme Self,
wherever the mind goes, there are states of meditative absorption.
For whom does every desired happiness of the mind ever come to pass?
Since everything is dependent on destiny, one should therefore take refuge in contentment. 14.
Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows, so too does whatever action has been performed follow after the doer. (15)
For one whose mind is unsettled, there is no happiness either among people or in the forest;
people burn through association, while the forest burns through the absence of attachment. 16.
For just as one finds water in the earth by digging with a spade, so too does one who is desirous of learning obtain knowledge residing in the teacher through service. (17)
The fruit of human beings depends upon their karma, and the intellect follows the course of karma;
nevertheless, the wise and noble act only after having reflected well. (18)
Contentment should be practiced in three matters: with one's own wife, in food, and in wealth;
yet it should not be practiced in three others: in study, in recitation, and in giving.
He who does not pay homage to the guru who has bestowed upon him even a single syllable will, after passing through a hundred births as a dog, be born among the Cāṇḍālas. (13.20)
At the end of an eon Mount Meru may shake, and at the end of a kalpa the seven oceans may overflow;
yet the virtuous never waver from the goal they have undertaken.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Cāṇakyanītidarpaṇa. ||13||
Chapter Fourteen:
On this earth there are three jewels—water, food, and well-spoken words. Only by the foolish is the designation "jewel" applied to fragments of stone. (1)
These are the fruits of the tree of one's own transgressions for embodied beings:
poverty, suffering, diseases, imprisonment, and calamities. (2)
Wealth can be regained, friends can be regained, a wife can be regained, and the earth can be regained;
all these may be obtained again and again, but the body cannot. (3)
Even a multitude of beings, though they may conquer their enemies, are like a rain-bearing cloud that is warded off even by mere blades of grass. (4)
Oil in water, a secret with a rogue, even a slight gift to a worthy recipient, and a scripture with a wise person—each expands of its own accord through the inherent power of the substance. (5)
If the state of mind that arises in a discourse on the Dharma, in a cremation ground, or among the sick were to remain forever, who would not be liberated from bondage? (6)
If one possessed such an understanding before as one has when remorse has arisen, who would not achieve great success? (7)
One should not feel astonishment at generosity, austerity, heroism, specialized knowledge, discipline, or statesmanship; for the earth abounds in many jewels. (8)
Even one who stands afar is not distant for him in whose mind that person dwells;
but he who is not in another's heart is far away, even if standing nearby. (9)
And because one who desires what is dear should always speak what is pleasant to that person;
the hunter sings a sweet-sounding song in order to kill the deer. (14.10)
Land that is too near leads to destruction, while land situated too far away does not yield fruit;
therefore, O best of kings, land should be acquired and bestowed [as a gift]. 11.
Fire, water, women, fools, serpents, and royal families—
these six must always be approached with great care, for they can take one's life instantly.
He lives who possesses virtues; he lives who possesses righteousness. The life of one devoid of virtue and righteousness is purposeless.
If you wish to bring the world under your control by a single deed, then restrain the cow from grazing before fifteen mouths [have appeared]. (14)
He who knows how to speak words appropriate to the occasion, affectionate words consistent with his power, and anger proportionate to his own strength—he is a wise man. 15.
A single object indeed is perceived in three ways:
as a corpse by yogis, as a beautiful woman by lovers, and as meat by dogs. (16)
A wise person should not disclose a well-proven medicine, a religious duty, a domestic secret, sexual intercourse, bad eating, or improper learning. (17)
The days are spent in silence by the cuckoos until their voice, which bestows joy upon all people, begins to flow. 18.
One should properly grasp the Dharma, wealth, grain, the words of the guru, and medicine; otherwise, one does not survive. (19)
Abandon association with the wicked; cultivate the company of the virtuous.
Perform meritorious deeds day and night; constantly remember impermanence.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Cāṇakyanītidarpaṇa. ||14||
Fifteenth Chapter:
For one whose heart has been melted with compassion toward all living beings, what need is there for knowledge or liberation through matted hair and the smearing of ashes? (1)
If a teacher awakens even a single syllable in a disciple, there is no wealth on earth that he could give to become free from his debt. ||2||
There are only two ways to deal with the wicked and with thorns:
either to crush their faces with shoes or to cast them far away.
One who wears tattered rags, bears stains upon his teeth,
eats excessively, speaks harshly,
and sleeps at sunrise or sunset—
If Śrī, the wielder of the discus, were to abandon him. ||4||
Friends, sons, wives, and well-wishers abandon one who is destitute of wealth;
yet they resort once again to that same person when he possesses riches.
For in this world, wealth is indeed the kinsman of man. ||5||
Wealth acquired by unjust means remains for ten years;
when the eleventh year arrives, it perishes along with its very roots.
What is improper for a master is proper [as a reproach] for a low person;
nectar was death to Rāhu, while poison became the ornament of Śaṅkara. (7)
That is true food which is the remnant of what has been eaten by the twice-born;
that is true friendship which is extended toward another;
that is true wisdom which does not commit evil.
That which is performed without hypocrisy is dharma. ||8||
The gem rolls at the feet while the glass is worn upon the head;
yet at the time of purchase and sale, the glass is glass and the gem is a gem.
The treatises are endless, the sciences are many, time is short, and obstacles are numerous; therefore,
one should practice that which constitutes the essence.
Just as a swan [extracts] milk from the midst of water. ||15.10||
He who eats without honoring a guest who has come from afar, who is weary from the road, and who has come to his house in vain, is indeed called a Cāṇḍāla. (11)
They recite the four Vedas and the treatises on Dharma many times over,
yet they do not know themselves at all, just as a ladle does not know the flavor of the food it stirs.
Blessed is the boat consisting of the twice-born, which is the opposite [of other boats] in the ocean of worldly existence;
all those who sit below it cross over, while those who remain on top fall down. 13.
This leader of medicinal herbs is a treasury of nectar,
and this moon possesses a body composed of nectar; yet, even though it is endowed with splendor,
it becomes devoid of rays upon reaching the orb of the sun.
Who does not fall into insignificance when settled in another's house? 14.
This bee, dwelling amidst the petals of a lotus and languid with intoxication from the nectar of the water-lily,
has by the power of fate arrived in a foreign land.
He highly values the juice of the *kuṭaja* flower. ||15||

By whom my father was struck on the soles of his feet in anger and turned yellow; by whom, out of wrath, my beloved wife—who had been kept by the best of Brahmins since childhood—was held in the cavity of her mouth as an enemy;
and who cut down my house every day for the purpose of worshipping Umā’s consort.
Therefore, O Lord, being constantly distressed, it is right for me to abandon this abode of the twice-born. (16)
Indeed, there are many kinds of bonds; yet the bond formed by the rope of affection is another.
Even the six-legged bee, though skilled at splitting wood, [cannot escape it].
It becomes motionless within the lotus bud. ||17||
On this earth, some great mountain was held effortlessly with two arms by You;
for that reason, You are constantly celebrated as Govardhana in heaven and on earth.
Yet, I carry You—the sustainer of the three worlds—on the tips of my breasts, and that is not counted.
Or what is the use of much speaking, O Keśava? Fame is obtained through meritorious deeds. ||18||
Some great mountain on earth, though exceedingly heavy, was held effortlessly by Your two arms;
for that reason, You are constantly celebrated as Govardhana in heaven and on earth.
Yet I carry You, the upholder of the three worlds, within the burden of my breasts—how can that be counted?
Or what is the use of much speaking, O Keśava? Fame is obtained through meritorious deeds. ||19||
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Cāṇakyanītidarpaṇa. ||15||
Sixteenth Chapter:

The state of the Lord has not been meditated upon according to the prescribed rule for the sake of severing the cycle of worldly existence, nor has that Dharma been acquired which is capable of splitting the door-panels of the gateway to heaven.
We have not even in a dream embraced the pair of full breasts and thighs of a woman;
we are merely axes for felling the forest of our mother’s youth. 1.
They speak with one man, look with amorous glances at another, and think of yet another in their hearts; for women, delight is never found in a single object.
That fool who, out of delusion, thinks, "This lustful woman is in love with me," will fall under her power and dance like a pet bird.
Who, having obtained wealth, has not become proud? To whom have calamities not befallen among those attached to sense-objects?
By whom on earth has the mind not been shattered by women? Who indeed is a favorite of the king? Who has not fallen within the range of Time (Death)? And what suppliant has attained dignity?
Or who, having fallen into the difficult terrain of the wicked, has traveled along the path in safety? ||4||
No one has ever fashioned such a golden doe, nor has one been seen before, nor even heard of;
yet, such is the thirst of the joy of the Raghus.
At the time of destruction, one's intellect becomes perverted. ||5||
One attains supremacy through virtues, not by sitting upon a high seat;
does a crow become a Garuda even when perched atop the pinnacle of a palace? (6)
Virtues are honored everywhere, not even great riches;
is the full moon so worthy of veneration as the waning moon when it is free from stain? (7)
One who is praised for virtues by others becomes virtuous even if he is devoid of virtue;
yet even Indra incurs lightness of reputation by proclaiming his own virtues.
Virtues attain a pleasing quality when they reach a person of discrimination;
indeed, a gem shines all the more when set in gold. (9)
Though equal to the Omniscient One in virtues, one who is alone and without support perishes;
even a priceless ruby requires gold as its setting. (16.10)

That wealth which is acquired through excessive hardship, that pleasure which is gained through excessive greed, and that livelihood which involves the oppression of others—none of these are found among the virtuous. (11)
What is the use of that fortune which is like a wife kept for oneself alone;
whereas that which is common to all, like a courtesan, is enjoyed even by travelers? (12)
Regarding wealth, life, women, and the act of eating, all living beings remain unsatisfied; they have gone, they will go, and they are going [to their deaths]. (13)
All forms of giving, sacrifices, fire-offerings, and ritual oblations eventually perish;
however, the gift of fearlessness to all embodied beings given to a worthy recipient never perishes. (14)
Grass is light; cotton is lighter than grass, and a beggar is even lighter than cotton.
Why has he not been carried away by the wind? He will surely beg from me. (15)
It is better to give up one's life than to live with the destruction of one's honor;
in the abandonment of life there is but a moment of pain, whereas in the loss of honor there is suffering day after day.
All living beings are pleased by the gift of pleasant words;
therefore, only such words should be spoken—what poverty can there be in speech? (17)
Of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra, there are two fruits comparable to nectar:
well-spoken words that are sweet to taste, and association with virtuous people. (18)
Whatever charity, study, or austerity was practiced in birth after birth, by that very force of habitual practice, the embodied soul practices them again. (19)
Knowledge that remains only in books and wealth that has passed into the hands of others is neither true knowledge nor real wealth when the time for action arises. (16.20)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Cāṇakyanītidarpaṇa*. ||16||
The seventeenth chapter:

Knowledge acquired through reliance on books alone is not truly learned if it has not been studied in the presence of a guru; such people do not shine in the midst of an assembly, like women who have conceived by an adulterer.
One should return a deed for a deed and violence for an act of violence;
no fault falls upon one who behaves wickedly toward a wicked person. (2)
Whatever is distant, whatever is difficult to attain, and whatever is situated far away—all that can be accomplished through austerity, for austerity is indeed difficult to surpass. (3)
If there is greed, what is the use of virtue? If there is malice, what is the use of sins?
If there is truth, what is the use of austerity? If the mind is pure, what is the use of a sacred pilgrimage site?
If there is goodness, what is the use of other qualities? If there is great majesty, what is the use of ornaments?
If true knowledge exists, what is the use of wealth? If infamy exists, what is the use of life? (4)
He whose father is Ratnākara and whose sister is Lakṣmī—Śaṅkha must wander for alms; what has not been given does not come to him.
One who is incapable may be virtuous, as may a student, one who is penniless, one afflicted by disease, a devotee of the gods, or an elderly woman devoted to her husband. (6)
There is no gift equal to food and water; no lunar day equal to the twelfth;
no mantra superior to the Gāyatrī; and no deity greater than one’s mother. (7)
The venom of Takṣaka is in his fang, that of the fly is in its head, and the venom of the scorpion is in its tail;
but the venom of the wicked man is in every limb.
For a woman who observes a fast or undertakes a vow without her husband's permission takes away the longevity of her husband; that woman shall go to hell. (9)
A woman is not purified by gifts, nor even by hundreds of fasts, nor likewise by visiting sacred fords, as she is by the water from her husband’s feet. (17.10)

Having drunk water that is the residue from a foot-washing, the residue from a drink, or likewise the residue from a twilight ritual, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; such water is equal to dog urine.
The hand is noble through generosity, not by a bracelet;
purity comes through bathing, not by sandalwood paste;
satisfaction arises from honor, not from food.
Liberation comes through knowledge, not through mere ornamentation. ||12||
One who has his hair shaved at a barber’s house, applies fragrant ointments on a stone,
or beholds his own reflection in water, would take away the splendor even of Indra.
The *tuṇḍī* plant instantly robs one of wisdom; the *vacā* plant instantly produces wisdom.
A woman instantly robs one of strength; milk instantly bestows strength. (14)
For those virtuous ones in whose hearts the desire to assist others remains awake, their misfortunes perish and prosperity attends them at every step. (15)
If one has a beautiful wife, if one has wealth, and if one has a son endowed with the quality of discipline—then what further excellence could there be in the city of the foremost of gods? (16)
Food, sleep, fear, and sexual intercourse—
these are common to humans and animals alike;
knowledge is the superior distinction of human beings.
Devoid of knowledge, they are equal to beasts. ||17||
If the bees seeking alms are driven away by the flapping of the ears of a noble elephant whose intellect is blinded by rut,
this is merely a loss of ornament for the pair of its temples.
The bees, moreover, dwell in the forest of blooming lotuses. ||18||
The king, the courtesan, Yama, fire, the thief, the child, and the beggar—these seven do not know the suffering of others; the eighth is the thorn of the village. 19.
"O young girl, what do you see down there? What has fallen upon the ground?
"O fool! Do you not realize that the pearl of youth has already passed away? (17.20)
O Ketakī, though you dwell among serpents, are incomplete, thorny,
crooked, born of the mud, and difficult to approach,
you are dear to all living beings by your fragrance.
Indeed, a single virtue destroys all faults. ||21||
Youth, the possession of wealth, power, and lack of discernment—each one alone leads to misfortune; how much more so when all four are present together? (22)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the Cāṇakyanītidarpaṇa. ||17||
